Newenham
NYOO-uhn-am
n. (a Cistercian abbey near Axminster in Devon, founded 1247 by Reginald and William de Mohun; one of the last of the order's English foundations)
Old English niwan hamm, the new enclosure or river-meadow — the new homestead by the Axe.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Newenham was founded in 1247 by the brothers Reginald and William de Mohun, a daughter of Beaulieu, and it was among the last Cistercian houses planted in England — more than a century after the great wave of the eleven-forties, when the order's first fervour was long spent and its best land taken. It was never rich, and it was dissolved with the rest. A latecomer among houses has an obvious text, and it is a parable about wages. The householder goes out “about the eleventh hour” (Mat 20:6) and finds men standing idle, and at the reckoning “when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny” (Mat 20:9) — the same as those who had borne the heat of the day. The parable is not about fairness in employment. It is about the murmuring of the early-hired against a generosity that costs them nothing, and it ends where the kingdom always ends: “So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen” (Mat 20:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hire as to procure from another person and for temporary use, at a certain price; and penny as an ancient denarius, a Roman coin, the eighth part of an ounce.

expand to see more

HIRE, v.t. To procure from another person and for temporary use, at a certain price, or for a stipulated or reasonable equivalent.

PENNY, n. An ancient English silver coin; but now an imaginary money of account. In Scripture, the denarius, a Roman coin.

IDLE, a. Not employed; unoccupied with business; inactive; doing nothing.

LABORER, n. One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill, as distinguished from an artisan.

MURMUR, v.i. To utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice; to utter sullen discontent.

Key Scripture

Mat 20:6 — "And about the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle, and saith unto them, Why stand ye here all the day idle?"

Mat 20:9 — "And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny."

Mat 20:11 — "And when they had received it, they murmured against the goodman of the house,"

Mat 20:16 — "So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen."

Modern Corruption

One of the last Cistercian houses in England, and the parable about being hired at the eleventh hour.

expand to see more

The corruption is the murmur of the early-hired, which is the oldest grievance inside the church and the hardest to name as sin because it dresses as justice. “they murmured against the goodman of the house” (Mat 20:11) is Matthew's word for men who had received exactly what they agreed to. Seniority, long service and early conversion generate a claim that the gospel does not recognise, and a late-founded house, like a late convert, is a standing provocation to it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that grace is not wages, and the parable is placed immediately after the rich young ruler and Peter's question about what the apostles would get. “for many be called, but few chosen” (Mat 20:16) closes the door on any arithmetic of merit. The eleventh-hour man does not receive less, and the first-hour man is not cheated; he is simply not the standard by which God gives.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English niwan hamm, the new enclosure; Greek misthoomai (G3409), to hire; Greek denarion (G1220), a penny; Greek argos (G692), idle; Greek gogguzo (G1111), to murmur.

expand to see more

Old English niwe + hamm — the new river-meadow enclosure.

Greek hora (G5610) — an hour; “about the eleventh hour” (Mat 20:6).

Greek argos (G692) — inactive, idle; “found others standing idle” (Mat 20:6).

Greek denarion (G1220) — a denarius, a day's wage; “received every man a penny” (Mat 20:9).

Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to mutter, to murmur; “they murmured against the goodman of the house” (Mat 20:11).

Usage

"“Why stand ye here all the day idle?” (Mat 20:6) — the question put to latecomers."

"“received every man a penny” (Mat 20:9) — the scandal of the parable."

"“So the last shall be first” (Mat 20:16) — the order of the kingdom."
